tagline: Mountain villages, wind-carved hoodoos and adobe churches along the High Road.
intro: The High Road to Taos winds through the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, linking high desert, small farms, forests and villages. New Mexico recognizes it as a state scenic byway, and the state tourism department highlights its mountain views, historic churches, Spanish villages and older Pueblo communities. Hoodoos mark the badlands, while the approach to Chimayó drops into a farming valley.

Las Trampas remained isolated except for travelers on the mountain road until the 1920s. Its land grant included common lands used for grazing and timber. After the U.S. conquest, land speculators and attorneys used the U.S. legal system to acquire the commons, which were sold to private owners in 1903. The former common lands became part of Carson National Forest in 1926; the High Road crosses the old grant today. Farther south, pavement reached Truchas only in the early 1970s.

From Pojoaque, travel toward Nambé on NM 503, then through the badlands to Chimayó. NM 76 climbs toward Truchas and continues through Las Trampas. Beyond Chamisal, NM 75 carries the journey through Peñasco and Vadito; NM 518 turns toward Talpa and Ranchos de Taos. The byway ends at NM 68, with San Francisco de Asís Church a few blocks south.

moments.title: El Santuario de Chimayó
moments.text: A small pit in a side room makes El Santuario de Chimayó a place of pilgrimage. Visitors take its tierra bendita, or holy dirt, in hope of healing. Bernardo Abeyta requested permission for a larger church in 1813; permission arrived in 1814, and the shrine replaced his earlier chapel by 1816. The adobe church has two bell towers and an entrance through a walled courtyard. Beside the dirt pit, a prayer room holds photographs, discarded crutches and other testimonials from people who claim to have been healed. The church takes no position on whether miracles have occurred there.
moments.notice: Two bell towers flank the adobe church beyond its walled courtyard.

moments.title: Truchas
moments.text: Water reached Truchas through hand-dug irrigation channels long before pavement reached the village. The farming settlement began with a Spanish land grant in 1754, on a mountain shoulder at 8,000 feet. Settlers built an acequia, an irrigation canal, several miles long to bring water from Truchas Peak to their crops. The grant required connected houses enclosing a plaza with a single entrance. A paved road finally entered in the early 1970s. The village later became a filming location for The Milagro Beanfield War, released in 1988. The village has views of the Truchas Peaks and Española Valley.

moments.title: Las Trampas
moments.text: San José de Gracia faces a dirt plaza beside NM 76, its adobe walls rising 34 feet. The church was completed in 1776, when Las Trampas had grown to 63 families. Its walls measure four to six feet thick, and a clerestory window above the nave directs sunlight toward the apse. The roof has been replaced several times, including work in 1932 by the Society for the Preservation of New Mexico Mission Churches. Las Trampas retains its early village layout, but the defensive wall that once enclosed it has disappeared.
moments.notice: The church faces the dirt plaza on the east side of NM 76.

moments.title: San Francisco de Asís
moments.text: San Francisco de Asís receives a new coat of earth each year, when community members and parishioners gather to replaster it. Its adobe buttresses include beehive curves at the ends of the transepts. Timber beams support the adobe roof, set in distinctive double corbels. Georgia O’Keeffe painted the church several times; Ansel Adams and Paul Strand photographed it. Maintaining it has also meant replacement: in 1967 the archdiocese renewed the roof and ceiling beams, installed replicas of the original corbels and replaced the doors with copies of their original design. The original sanctuary woodwork remained in place.
